Allentown, Pennsylvania :: Climate :: part 01 :: chunk_0020
Main article: [Climate of Allentown, Pennsylvania](/wiki/Climate_of_Allentown,_Pennsylvania "Climate of Allentown, Pennsylvania")

Under the [Köppen climate classification](/wiki/K%C3%B6ppen_climate_classification "Köppen climate classification"), Allentown falls within the [hot-summer humid continental climate](/wiki/Humid_continental_climate "Humid continental climate") (*Dfa*) if the 0 °C (32 °F) isotherm is used or the [humid subtropical climate](/wiki/Humid_subtropical_climate "Humid subtropical climate") (*Cfa*) if the −3 °C (27 °F) isotherm is used. Summers are typically warm and muggy. Fall and spring are generally mild. Winter is cool to cold. Precipitation is almost uniformly distributed throughout the year.

The average temperature in January is 30.1 °F (−1.1 °C) and the lowest officially recorded temperature was −15 °F (−26 °C) on [January 21, 1994](/wiki/1994_North_American_cold_wave "1994 North American cold wave").[[56]](#cite_note-nws-56) July averages 75.6 °F (24.2 °C) and the highest temperature on record was 105 °F (41 °C) on July 3, 1966.[[56]](#cite_note-nws-56)[[57]](#cite_note-57) January temperatures average below freezing. Seven months average above 50 °F (10.0 °C), and two months average above 71.6 °F (22.0 °C).

Snowfall is variable with some winters bringing light snow and others bringing multiple and significant snowstorms. Average snowfall is 33.1 inches (84 cm) seasonally[[58]](#cite_note-58) with February receiving the highest snowfall at just under 11 inches (280 mm). Rainfall is generally spread throughout the year with eight to 12 days of precipitation monthly[[59]](#cite_note-59) at an average annual rate of 43.5 inches (110.5 cm).[[60]](#cite_note-60) Allentown falls under the [U.S. Department of Agriculture](/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Agriculture "United States Department of Agriculture")'s 6b Plant [hardiness zone](/wiki/Hardiness_zone "Hardiness zone").[[61]](#cite_note-61)

The playing of team ball games (almost certainly including football) was first recorded in London by William FitzStephen around 1174–1183. He described the activities of London youths during the annual festival of [Shrove Tuesday](/wiki/Shrove_Tuesday "Shrove Tuesday").

:   "After lunch all of the city's youth would go out into the fields to take part in a ball game. The students of each school have their own ball; the workers from each city craft are also carrying their balls. Older citizens, fathers, and the wealthy would come on horseback to watch their juniors competing, and to relive their own youth vicariously: you can see their inner passions aroused as they watch the action and get caught up in the fun being had by the carefree adolescents."[[3]](#cite_note-4)

Regular references to the game occurred throughout the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, including the first reference to the word "football" in English when it was outlawed by King [Henry IV of England](/wiki/Henry_IV_of_England "Henry IV of England") in 1409. Early games were probably disorganised and violent. In the sixteenth century, the headmaster of [St Paul's School](/wiki/St_Paul%27s_School_(London) "St Paul's School (London)") [Richard Mulcaster](/wiki/Richard_Mulcaster "Richard Mulcaster") is credited with taking [mob football](/wiki/Mob_football "Mob football") and transforming it into organised and refereed team football. In 1581 he wrote about his game of football, which included smaller teams, referees, set positions and even a coach.

The Empire State Building was the world's tallest building until the [North Tower](/wiki/1_World_Trade_Center_(1970%E2%80%932001) "1 World Trade Center (1970–2001)") of the [World Trade Center](/wiki/World_Trade_Center_(1973%E2%80%932001) "World Trade Center (1973–2001)") was [topped out in 1970](/wiki/Construction_of_the_World_Trade_Center "Construction of the World Trade Center"); following the [September 11 attacks](/wiki/Collapse_of_the_World_Trade_Center "Collapse of the World Trade Center") in 2001, the Empire State Building was once more New York City's tallest building until it was surpassed in 2012 by [One World Trade Center](/wiki/One_World_Trade_Center "One World Trade Center"). As of 2025, the building is the [eighth-tallest building in New York City](/wiki/List_of_tallest_buildings_in_New_York_City "List of tallest buildings in New York City"), the [tenth-tallest completed skyscraper in the United States](/wiki/List_of_tallest_buildings_in_the_United_States "List of tallest buildings in the United States"), and the [59th-tallest completed skyscraper in the world](/wiki/List_of_tallest_buildings "List of tallest buildings").

The hyperboloid structure itself is a result of 16 identical assembled concrete columns. There is controversy as to what these columns, having hyperbolic section and weighing 90 t, represent, some say they are two hands moving upwards to heaven, others associate it to the chalice Jesus used in the last supper and some claim it represent his crown of thorns. Including revenue from the 2012, 2017 and 2023 reissues, *Titanic* earned $674.3 million in North America and $1.590 billion in other countries, for a worldwide total of $2.264 billion.[[151]](#cite_note-BoxOfficeBOM-152) It became the [highest-grossing film of all time worldwide](/wiki/Highest-grossing_film_of_all_time_worldwide "Highest-grossing film of all time worldwide") in 1998, beating *[Jurassic Park](/wiki/Jurassic_Park "Jurassic Park")* (1993).[[152]](#cite_note-153) The film remained so for twelve years, until *[Avatar](/wiki/Avatar_(2009_film) "Avatar (2009 film)")* (2009), also written and directed by Cameron, surpassed it in 2010.[[153]](#cite_note-newsday-154) It would hold the record for being Paramount's highest-grossing film domestically until it was dethroned by *[Top Gun: Maverick](/wiki/Top_Gun:_Maverick "Top Gun: Maverick")* (2022) twenty-five years later.[[154]](#cite_note-155) On March 1, 1998,[[155]](#cite_note-156) it became the first film to earn more than $1 billion worldwide[[156]](#cite_note-157) and on the weekend April 13–15, 2012—a century after the original vessel's foundering, *Titanic* became the second film to cross the $2 billion threshold during its 3D re-release.[[157]](#cite_note-158) [Box Office Mojo](/wiki/Box_Office_Mojo "Box Office Mojo") estimates that *Titanic* is the [fifth-highest-grossing film](/wiki/List_of_highest-grossing_films_in_Canada_and_the_United_States "List of highest-grossing films in Canada and the United States") of all time in North America when adjusting for ticket price inflation.[[158]](#cite_note-159) The site also estimates that the film sold over 128 million tickets in the US in its initial theatrical run.[[159]](#cite_note-160)

*Titanic* was the first foreign-language film to succeed in India, which claims to have the largest movie-going audience in the world.[[160]](#cite_note-161) A *[Hindustan Times](/wiki/Hindustan_Times "Hindustan Times")* report attributes this to its similarities and shared themes with most [Bollywood](/wiki/Bollywood "Bollywood") films.[[161]](#cite_note-162)
